motivation_letter.name: Goonja Gandhi
paragraphs: Karumi's core problem is compelling: demos happen too late in the buyer journey, and when they do, they're static and one-size-fits-all. Your solution—an agentic system that delivers hyper-personalized, 24/7 product demonstrations—inverts that dynamic. Rather than waiting for a sales team to respond to intent signals, your agents reach customers at the moment they're most receptive, in their language, with context pulled from their CRM history. I was drawn to this because it sits at an intersection I find technically interesting: real-time personalization, multi-language systems, CRM integration, and AI agents that must maintain coherence across a conversation while staying aligned with product knowledge.

Over five years as a frontend engineer, I've built features that require this kind of integration depth. At TCS, I led frontend architecture across enterprise applications where efficient state management and API integration directly reduced latency by 40% and improved responsiveness. More recently, I engineered NewsAlign, a fact-verification system using RAG pipelines, FAISS vector search, and LangChain, which forced me to think beyond simple LLM wrapping—to understand how retrieval, reasoning, and cost constraints interact. I've also spent deliberate time understanding the mechanics beneath abstractions: custom reactive engines, component scaffolding, performance optimization down to bundle size (68% reduction through code splitting), and accessibility standards applied at scale. This habit of asking 'what problem is this abstraction solving' has shaped how I approach systems.

The Product Engineer role requires someone comfortable across the stack, and my trajectory reflects that. My frontend foundation is solid—React, Next.js, TypeScript, React Server Components, SSR/SSG/ISR optimizations, Lighthouse scores from 73 to 95. But I've also worked backend-adjacent: Node.js, GraphQL, REST APIs, database design thinking. For Karumi specifically, the full-stack nature matters because the agent experience depends on frontend responsiveness (conversation flow, personalization rendering), backend reliability (CRM sync, conversation persistence), and the bridge between them (SSE streaming, state coherence, multi-language context handling). I'm comfortable moving fluidly across those boundaries rather than owning only one layer.

I'm drawn to roles where the product challenge and the engineering challenge are inseparable. At Karumi, they are: the value of your platform lives in whether agents feel responsive, maintain context, handle language switching seamlessly, and integrate cleanly with the customer's CRM. Those are engineering problems. I want to work on a team that treats them that way. Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to the opportunity to discuss how I can contribute.
motivation_letter.closing: Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to the opportunity to discuss how I can contribute.

summary: Robotics data infrastructure and live system integration, Full-Stack Engineer role, end-to-end feature ownership from capture dashboards to data pipelines

motivation_letter.name: Goonja Gandhi
paragraphs: What strikes me about Revel is the deliberate movement of responsibility to the edge—capturing data directly from robotic systems, designing the communication layer that connects vision and voice, and building the entire pipeline from device through to training infrastructure. This is the inverse of many applications I've built, which abstract away the underlying systems. At Revel, the abstraction breaks down, and you have to own it completely. That appeals to me because I've spent years asking what lies beneath the frameworks I use, and this role seems to demand exactly that kind of thinking across the entire stack.

My frontend background at TCS and Datapret has given me experience with complex state management, real-time responsiveness, and the kind of architectural decisions that scale—particularly around caching strategies, bundle optimization, and rendering efficiency. But over the past year, I've deliberately expanded beyond frontend by building NewsAlign, an AI-powered fact verification system where I engineered the complete pipeline: semantic search with FAISS, LLM reasoning, backend API design, and deployment. That project taught me that frontend excellence is hollow without understanding the data flow that feeds it. I reduced bundle size by 68% and lifted the Lighthouse score to 95, but the more valuable lesson was recognizing that a capture dashboard is only useful if the backend architecture and data pipeline are sound.

What makes me suited for this role is that I'm neither a pure frontend engineer forced into backend, nor a backend engineer uncomfortable with UI. I've built internal tools, optimized performance across the full stack, and worked with GraphQL, REST APIs, and system design—but I'm genuinely interested in the robotic communication layer, the data labeling workflow, and the infrastructure that connects devices to training clusters. The fact that you're asking someone to own features end-to-end, from UI to backend, suggests you value engineers who can reason about trade-offs across the entire system rather than optimize locally. That's the kind of engineer I've become.

I'm drawn to Revel because the technical challenges are not abstractions; they're concrete problems about how systems communicate, how data moves, and how humans interact with machines. I want to build capture dashboards that are responsive and intuitive, but I want to understand the communication bottleneck that makes them lag. I want to implement live data overlays, but I want to know how the streaming architecture works beneath the UI. Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to the opportunity to discuss how I can contribute.
motivation_letter.closing: Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to the opportunity to discuss how I can contribute.
